laws.name: Alabama Personal Data Protection Act
laws.threshold: Businesses that operate in Alabama or target Alabama residents and either control or process the personal data of more than 25,000 Alabama consumers (not counting data processed solely to complete a payment transaction), or get more than 25% of gross revenue from selling personal data (no consumer minimum). Businesses with fewer than 500 employees, and nonprofits with fewer than 100 employees, are exempt if they don't sell personal data.
laws.summary: Alabama's comprehensive privacy law, signed April 17, 2026 and effective May 1, 2027. It covers businesses handling data of more than 25,000 Alabama consumers, or getting more than 25% of revenue from data sales, but businesses under 500 employees that don't sell personal data are exempt. Opt-in consent for sensitive data, COPPA-compliant handling of data from known children under 13, and consent before selling or targeting ads to known teens 13 to 15. Unlike most state laws, there's no appeal right and no data protection assessment requirement. The Attorney General enforces with a 45-day cure period that doesn't expire; civil penalties up to $15,000 per violation.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice listing data categories, purposes, data shared with third parties, how to contact you, and how to exercise rights
- Clear disclosure if you sell personal data or use it for targeted advertising
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, and portability with a 45-day response clock (one 45-day extension with notice); no new account required to submit
- Clear and conspicuous opt-out link (or up-to-date contact info) for sale and targeted advertising, plus opt-out of profiling for solely automated significant decisions
- If an opt-out preference signal conflicts with a user's existing setting or loyalty program, follow the signal (you may notify them of the conflict and let them confirm)
- Opt-in consent before processing sensitive data, with a way to revoke consent
- Handle data from known children under 13 per COPPA
- Consent before selling or targeting ads to consumers you know are 13 to 15
- No denying service or changing price because someone opted out (bona fide loyalty programs are allowed)
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you

laws.name: American Privacy Rights Act
laws.threshold: Entities subject to FTC jurisdiction that collect or process covered data; small businesses (under $40M revenue, under 200K consumers) largely exempt
laws.summary: Bipartisan federal privacy bill introduced in 2024 that passed committee but stalled on the House floor. Would establish a national baseline with data minimization, consumer rights, private right of action, and preemption of most state privacy laws. APRA hasn't been reintroduced in the 119th Congress. The likeliest successor is House Republicans' SECURE Data Act (H.R. 8413), introduced April 22, 2026. It would preempt almost all state privacy laws and be enforced by the FTC and state AGs. A subcommittee hearing was held June 3, 2026, but no markup has been scheduled, and the 119th Congress ends January 3, 2027.
laws.build: Not law. Nothing here is required today. Design ahead by collecting only the data each feature needs; data minimization is the core of every federal proposal and already law in Maryland.

laws.name: California Consumer Privacy Act
laws.enforcer: California Attorney General / California Privacy Protection Agency
laws.threshold: For-profit businesses doing business in California that meet any: annual gross revenue over $26,625,000 in the preceding calendar year (the $25M threshold as CPI-adjusted, in effect for 2025 and 2026; next adjustment January 1, 2027); buy, sell, or share the personal information of 100,000 or more California consumers or households a year; or derive 50% or more of annual revenue from selling or sharing personal information
laws.summary: California's privacy law, expanded by the CPRA (one statute; this record covers both). Covers sharing for cross-context advertising, not just sales. The CPPA's regulations finalized in September 2025 (effective January 1, 2026) add risk assessments (for processing already underway, due by December 31, 2027), cybersecurity audits for larger businesses (first certifications due April 1, 2028 to April 1, 2030 depending on revenue), and rules for automated decision-making technology (ADMT compliance from January 1, 2027). Limited private right of action for data breaches.
laws.build:
- "Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information" link in the footer (or one combined opt-out link)
- "Limit the Use of My Sensitive Personal Information" link if you use sensitive data beyond what's needed to provide the service
- Treat Global Privacy Control (GPC) browser signals as a valid opt-out, with no extra steps
- Notice at collection shown at or before the point data is collected (sign-up forms, SDKs, apps)
- Privacy policy updated at least every 12 months, including retention periods per data category
- At least two ways to submit requests (online-only businesses: email plus a web form or portal from January 1, 2027 under SB 923); confirm receipt within 10 business days, respond within 45 days, process opt-outs within 15 business days
- Access, deletion, correction, and portability workflows with identity verification
- No dark patterns: opting out can't take more steps than opting in
- Data minimization: collect only what is reasonably necessary for disclosed purposes
- Risk assessments before high-risk processing; ADMT notice and opt-out for significant decisions from January 1, 2027
- CCPA-compliant contracts with service providers, contractors, and third parties
- No penalty or degraded service for exercising rights (financial incentives need a notice)
laws.next: January 1, 2027: automated decision-making technology (ADMT) notice, opt-out and access rules apply. Also January 1, 2027 (SB 923): the deletion right covers personal information collected about a consumer from any source, including data brokers and partners, and online-only businesses must offer a web form or portal for requests, not just email. January 1, 2027: revenue threshold and penalty amounts get their next CPI adjustment. January 1, 2027 (AB 566): browsers must offer a built-in opt-out preference signal, so expect more GPC-style signals. December 31, 2027: risk assessments due for high-risk processing that began before 2026. April 1, 2028: first risk assessment submissions to the CPPA and first cybersecurity audit certifications for businesses with over $100M revenue ($50M-$100M: April 1, 2029; under $50M: April 1, 2030).

laws.name: Children's Online Privacy Protection Act
laws.threshold: Operators of websites/online services directed to children under 13, or with actual knowledge of collecting data from children under 13
laws.summary: Federal law restricting online collection of personal information from children under 13. Requires verifiable parental consent before collecting, using, or disclosing a child's personal information. Operators must post clear privacy notices, allow parents to review and delete their child's data, and maintain reasonable data security. The FTC's amended COPPA Rule (first update since 2013) became enforceable April 22, 2026: it requires separate parental consent before disclosing children's data to third parties such as advertisers, a written data retention policy, and a written children's information security program. FTC enforces; no private right of action. COPPA 2.0 (teen coverage) passed the Senate in March 2026 but is not law.
laws.build:
- Neutral age screen that doesn't nudge kids to lie about their age
- Verifiable parental consent before collecting any personal information from children under 13
- Separate parental consent before disclosing children's data to third parties such as advertisers (amended rule, enforceable April 22, 2026)
- Direct notice to parents and an online privacy notice describing data practices
- Parent dashboard or process to review, delete, and revoke consent for their child's data
- Written data retention policy; delete children's data once it's no longer needed
- Written children's information security program
- Don't require more data than reasonably necessary for a child to participate

laws.name: Children's Online Privacy Protection Act 2.0
laws.threshold: As proposed: operators of websites and online services directed to children under 13 or teens under 17, or with actual knowledge (or knowledge fairly implied) of users under 17
laws.summary: NOT LAW. The Children and Teens' Online Privacy Protection Act (S. 836) passed the Senate unanimously on March 5, 2026. On June 29, 2026 the House passed its own package, the KIDS Act (H.R. 7757), 267-117. The KIDS Act builds on COPPA 2.0: it covers children under 14 and teens 14 to 17, applies when an operator knows or should have known a user's age, and bans targeted advertising to minors. The two chambers haven't reconciled their bills, and the 119th Congress ends January 3, 2027. Product teams should design for it but are not yet bound by it. The binding change this year is the FTC's amended COPPA Rule (see COPPA record), enforceable April 22, 2026.
laws.build:
Not law. Nothing here is required today. If you want to design ahead of it:
- Build age signals into your product so you can identify users under 17
- Architect ad systems so targeted ads can be switched off for minors
- Build an 'eraser button' so parents and teens can delete teen data
Several states (Connecticut, Delaware, Maryland, New Jersey, Oregon, Colorado) already restrict targeted ads and data sales for known minors, so much of this is required at the state level now.

laws.name: Colorado Privacy Act
laws.threshold: Controllers doing business in Colorado that control or process personal data of 100,000+ Colorado consumers in a calendar year, or 25,000+ consumers and derive any revenue or receive a discount on goods or services from selling personal data. Any controller processing biometric data is covered for that data, and minors' protections apply regardless of volume.
laws.summary: Colorado's comprehensive privacy law, effective July 1, 2023. Grants residents rights to access, correct, delete, port data, and opt out of sale, targeted advertising, and profiling. Requires data protection assessments for high-risk processing and opt-in consent for sensitive data. Universal opt-out mechanisms (like GPC) must be honored as of July 1, 2024. 2024-2025 amendments added biometric data rules (July 1, 2025), protections for minors under 18 that apply regardless of volume (October 1, 2025), and precise geolocation as sensitive data (2025). The general 60-day cure period ended January 1, 2025. AG and district attorneys enforce; no private right of action.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice meeting Colorado's rule-specified content requirements
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, and portability with a 45-day response clock and appeal process
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and profiling; honor universal opt-out signals such as GPC
- Opt-in consent before processing or selling sensitive data (which now includes precise geolocation and neural/biological data), with refresh of consent at set intervals per the Colorado rules
- No dark patterns in consent flows
- Data protection assessment before high-risk processing, kept on file
- Minors under 18 (since Oct 1, 2025, at any volume) when you know or willfully disregard that a user is a minor: get consent (a parent's for under 13) before targeted ads, sale, significant-decision profiling, engagement-extending design features, or precise geolocation collection; limit use and retention to what's needed; assess heightened risk of harm to minors
- Biometric data (since July 1, 2025): written retention and deletion policy and consent, regardless of the user-count threshold
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you
laws.next: December 31, 2026: the 60-day cure period for minors' data violations ends. January 1, 2027: Colorado's automated decision-making law (SB 26-189, which repealed and replaced the Colorado AI Act) is set to take effect, requiring pre-use notices, adverse-outcome notices and human review rights for automated consequential decisions; it's a separate statute from the CPA, and enforcement may slip pending AG rulemaking and the xAI lawsuit.

checker.dutyBelow: Minors' data rules (since October 1, 2025) apply to any controller doing business in Colorado regardless of volume, and biometric data rules (since July 1, 2025) apply to any controller that processes any biometric identifiers.

req.cure: Ended January 1, 2025 for most violations; a 60-day cure still applies to minors' data violations until December 31, 2026

laws.name: Connecticut Data Privacy Act
laws.threshold: As amended by SB 1295 (effective July 1, 2026): controllers that, in the preceding calendar year, controlled or processed data of 35,000+ Connecticut consumers, OR control or process any sensitive data, OR offer any personal data for sale (data processed solely to complete a payment transaction doesn't count toward the first two). The old 100K and 25K/25%-revenue prongs are gone.
laws.summary: Connecticut's comprehensive privacy law, effective July 1, 2023. SB 1295 (effective July 1, 2026) lowered the threshold to 35K consumers and now covers anyone processing sensitive data or selling personal data regardless of volume. It added rights to contest profiling decisions and to get a list of third parties that bought the consumer's data, added neural data, financial credentials and government ID numbers to sensitive data, and requires privacy notices to disclose whether data trains LLMs. SB 4 (effective October 1, 2026) bans selling precise geolocation data and extends the deletion right to some publicly available data and inferences; data broker registration starts January 1, 2027. SB 1295 also bans targeted ads to and sale of data about known minors under 18. Opt-in for sensitive data; universal opt-out signals honored. AG enforces; fines up to $5,000 per willful violation.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice stating whether personal data is used to train large language models, request methods, and month/year last updated
- Request flow for access (including inferences), correction, deletion, and portability with a 45-day clock and appeal process
- List of third parties that bought a consumer's data, available on request
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and significant-decision profiling; honor GPC and other universal opt-out signals
- Opt-in consent for sensitive data, which now includes neural data, financial account credentials, and government ID numbers
- Profiling decisions with legal or similar effects: where feasible, explain the reason, let users review data and contest the result (for housing decisions, correct data and get a reevaluation), and run an impact assessment for profiling started on or after August 1, 2026
- Users 13 to 17 (since July 1, 2026): if you know or willfully disregard a user's age, no targeted advertising and no sale of their data, even with consent
- From October 1, 2026: do not sell precise geolocation data
- Never return SSNs, account numbers, or similar identifiers in access responses
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you
laws.next: January 1, 2027: data broker registration begins ($2,500 a year). July 1, 2028: state deletion mechanism for data brokers due; brokers must process deletion requests every 45 days from October 1, 2028.

laws.name: Delaware Personal Data Privacy Act
laws.threshold: Controllers processing data of 35K+ DE consumers/year (excluding data processed solely to complete a payment transaction), or 10K+ DE consumers/year and deriving more than 20% of gross revenue from personal data sales (lower thresholds than most states)
laws.summary: Delaware's comprehensive privacy law, effective January 1, 2025. Low thresholds (35K consumers). Opt-in consent for sensitive data and consent before selling or targeting ads to known teens 13-17. Consumers can get a list of the categories of third parties that received their data (specific third parties from January 1, 2027). Universal opt-out signals required from January 1, 2026. The 60-day cure period ran through 2025 and is now at the AG's discretion. Civil penalties up to $10,000 per willful violation.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice listing data categories, purposes, third parties, and how to exercise rights
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, and portability with a 45-day clock and appeal process
- List of the categories of third parties that received a consumer's data, available on request (specific third parties from January 1, 2027)
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and profiling; honor universal opt-out signals (required from January 1, 2026)
- Opt-in consent for sensitive data
- Consent before selling or targeting ads to consumers you know are 13-17
- Data protection assessment before targeted ads, data sales, risky profiling, or sensitive-data processing (if you process data of 100,000+ Delaware consumers; 50,000+ from January 1, 2027)
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you
laws.next: January 1, 2027: HB 380 lowers coverage to 10,000 Delaware consumers, or 5,000 with more than 20% of revenue from data sales. The assessment threshold drops from 100,000 to 50,000 consumers, and a new impact assessment applies to profiling for automated decisions. Consumers can get a list of specific third parties (not just categories), and the law also reaches third parties that acquire data from controllers. Sensitive data adds inferences, national origin, neural data, financial account data and government ID numbers. Teen opt-in extends to profiling, and selling sensitive data needs consent plus prior notice.

laws.name: Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act
laws.enforcer: U.S. Department of Education (Student Privacy Policy Office)
laws.threshold: Educational agencies and institutions that receive federal funding from the U.S. Department of Education
laws.summary: Federal law protecting the privacy of student education records. Gives parents (and students over 18) rights to access, review, and request amendment of education records. Schools generally cannot disclose education records without written consent, with exceptions (school officials, transfer schools, financial aid, judicial orders, health/safety emergencies). Enforced by withholding federal funds; no private right of action.
laws.build:
Applies to schools; ed-tech vendors are bound through the school contract (the 'school official' exception).
- Use student records only for the purpose the school authorized
- No re-disclosure of student records to other parties without school authorization
- No advertising or profiling using student education records
- Let the school control the data: support access, amendment, and deletion requests routed through the school
- Delete or return student data at contract end
- Check state student privacy laws too (California SOPIPA and similar), which often add stricter vendor rules

laws.name: Florida Digital Bill of Rights
laws.enforcer: Florida Attorney General (Department of Legal Affairs)
laws.threshold: For-profit businesses that do business in Florida, collect consumers' personal data and decide how it's processed, make more than $1 billion in global gross annual revenue, and also (a) get 50% or more of global gross annual revenue from selling online ads, including targeted ads, (b) operate a consumer smart speaker and voice command service with an integrated virtual assistant connected to a cloud service that uses hands-free verbal activation (vehicle devices from automakers excluded), or (c) operate an app store or digital distribution platform with at least 250,000 different apps. Affiliates that control or are controlled by such a business are covered too. Two duties reach further: any for-profit business doing business in Florida that collects personal data needs consent and a posted notice to sell sensitive data, and online platforms (social media, online games) likely to be predominantly accessed by children under 18 face separate restrictions regardless of size.
laws.summary: Florida's privacy law, effective July 1, 2024. Full duties reach only a handful of very large companies: over $1 billion in global revenue plus a big online ad business, a voice-assistant smart speaker, or an app store with 250,000+ apps. But any for-profit business that collects Floridians' personal data needs consent before selling sensitive data and must post "NOTICE: This website may sell your sensitive personal data." A separate section (s. 501.1735) restricts how social media and online game platforms likely to be predominantly accessed by kids under 18 profile children and collect their data, at any size. Unusual features: an opt-out of collection through voice or facial recognition, a ban on using device voice, face or video features for surveillance when not in active use, a retention schedule with a 2-year outer limit, and a ranking-factor disclosure for search engines. The Attorney General enforces exclusively, with civil penalties up to $50,000 per violation, tripled for violations involving known children, failing to delete or correct after a request, or continuing to sell or share after an opt-out. A 45-day cure period is at the AG's discretion and never applies to known-child violations. No private right of action and no universal opt-out signal requirement. First big case: the AG sued Roku in October 2025 over children's data; it settled June 26, 2026 with no fine and an estimated $25 million in child-protection engineering.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice, updated at least once a year, listing data categories (including sensitive data), purposes, categories shared and third parties, how to exercise rights and appeal, and your request methods
- If you sell sensitive data, post the exact notice "NOTICE: This website may sell your sensitive personal data." (applies to any for-profit business collecting personal data, not just $1B+ controllers); biometric sales need "NOTICE: This website may sell your biometric personal data."
- Clear disclosure of any sale or targeted advertising and how to opt out
- At least two secure, reliable request methods, without forcing anyone to create a new account
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, and portability with a 45-day clock (one 15-day extension if you tell the consumer within the first 45 days) and an appeal answered in writing within 60 days
- Let a parent or guardian exercise rights for a known child
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, profiling with legal or similarly significant effects, sensitive data processing, and collection through voice or facial recognition features
- Opt-in consent before processing sensitive data; known children 13-17 must give affirmative authorization, and under-13 data must follow COPPA
- Consent before selling sensitive data (applies to any for-profit business collecting personal data)
- Don't use a device's voice recognition, facial recognition, video or audio recording features for surveillance when the consumer isn't actively using them, unless they expressly allow it
- Retention schedule that stops using or keeping personal data once the purpose is met, the contract ends, or 2 years after the consumer's last interaction, unless an exemption applies
- Data protection assessment for targeted advertising, sales, risky profiling, sensitive data, and other heightened-risk processing
- If you run a search engine, publish a plain-language description of your main ranking factors, including any political or ideological weighting
- If you run a social media platform or online game likely to be predominantly accessed by under-18s (any size): no harmful processing or unnecessary profiling of children, no unnecessary collection or precise geolocation, a visible signal while collecting geolocation, and no dark patterns
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you

checker.dutyBelow: Florida's full law covers only companies with over $1 billion in global revenue that also run a large online ad business, a voice-assistant smart speaker or a 250,000-app store, so confirm whether you meet that test; even if you don't, any for-profit business selling Floridians' sensitive data needs consent and a posted notice, and kid-focused social media and gaming platforms have separate duties.

laws.name: General Data Protection Regulation
laws.threshold: Any org processing EU resident personal data, regardless of where the org is located
laws.summary: Landmark EU regulation establishing comprehensive data protection rights. Requires lawful basis for processing, data minimization, and purpose limitation. Imposes strict breach notification (72 hrs), DPIAs for high-risk processing, and appointment of DPOs. Fines up to 4% global annual revenue or €20M. On October 8, 2026 the Dutch DPA fined Uber €824,990,000 for fully automated driver deactivations (Art. 22) and poor transparency (Art. 13); Uber has appealed. The proposed digital omnibus changes to GDPR and cookie rules aren't law, and the Council hasn't adopted a negotiating mandate.
laws.build:
- Document a lawful basis (consent, contract, legitimate interests, etc.) for each processing purpose before launch
- Cookie consent banner: no non-essential cookies or trackers until the user opts in (ePrivacy rules), with reject as easy as accept
- Privacy notice meeting Articles 13-14
- Request flow for access, deletion, correction, portability, restriction, and objection, answered within one month
- Records of processing activities (Article 30)
- DPIA before high-risk processing (large-scale profiling, sensitive data, systematic monitoring)
- Data processing agreements with every vendor; Standard Contractual Clauses or EU-US Data Privacy Framework certification for transfers to the US
- Breach detection and a process to notify the regulator within 72 hours
- Privacy by design and default: minimal data collection and privacy-protective settings out of the box
- EU representative if you have no EU establishment; DPO if required

laws.name: Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act
laws.enforcer: FTC, federal banking regulators (OCC, FDIC, Fed, NCUA)
laws.threshold: Financial institutions that are significantly engaged in financial activities and their affiliates
laws.summary: Federal law requiring financial institutions to explain data-sharing practices and protect customer financial information. Three main rules: Financial Privacy Rule (annual privacy notices, opt-out of sharing with non-affiliates); Safeguards Rule (information security program — significantly updated in 2023); Pretexting Rule (prohibits social engineering to access financial records). No private right of action; enforced by FTC and banking regulators.
laws.build:
- Initial privacy notice at account opening, and annual notices unless you qualify for the exception
- Opt-out before sharing customer data with nonaffiliated third parties (with listed exceptions)
- Safeguards Rule: written information security program run by a named qualified individual
- Encryption of customer information in transit and at rest, and MFA for anyone accessing it
- Written risk assessment, regular testing, and vendor oversight
- Notify the FTC within 30 days of discovering a breach affecting 500 or more consumers
- No pretexting: build identity checks so callers can't social-engineer account data

laws.name: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act
laws.threshold: Covered entities (health plans, providers, clearinghouses) and their business associates
laws.summary: Federal law protecting health information (PHI) held by covered entities and their business associates. Privacy Rule sets standards for PHI use and disclosure; Security Rule requires administrative, physical, and technical safeguards for electronic PHI. Breach Notification Rule requires notice to individuals, HHS, and sometimes media. No private right of action — enforcement by HHS OCR with civil and criminal penalties.
laws.build:
- Signed Business Associate Agreement with every vendor that touches PHI (cloud hosting, analytics, support tools, AI vendors)
- Access controls, unique user IDs, audit logs, and encryption for electronic PHI
- Use and show only the minimum necessary PHI for each function
- Patient access requests fulfilled within 30 days, in the format requested where feasible
- Do not send PHI to advertising or analytics pixels and SDKs without a BAA
- Written risk analysis and risk management plan under the Security Rule
- Breach notification to individuals within 60 days of discovery

laws.name: Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act
laws.enforcer: Private right of action (no state agency enforces)
laws.threshold: Private entities that collect, capture, purchase, receive, or otherwise obtain biometric identifiers or information from Illinois residents
laws.summary: Illinois law governing collection and use of biometric identifiers (fingerprints, retina/iris scans, voiceprints, face geometry, hand scans). Requires a public written retention and destruction policy, written notice and a written release (electronic signatures count since August 2, 2024) before collection, and prohibits selling, leasing, trading, or otherwise profiting from biometric data. Private right of action for any aggrieved person: liquidated damages of $1,000 (negligent) or $5,000 (intentional or reckless), or actual damages if greater, plus attorneys' fees; no showing of actual harm needed (Rosenbach, 2019). A 2024 amendment (SB 2979, P.A. 103-0769, effective August 2, 2024) makes repeated collection of the same biometric from the same person by the same method one violation with at most one recovery (same for repeated disclosure to the same recipient). The Seventh Circuit held on April 1, 2026 (Clay v. Union Pacific) that this limit applies to cases pending when it was enacted. Claims have a five-year statute of limitations (Tims v. Black Horse Carriers, Ill. 2023). Has generated massive class action litigation.
laws.build:
Applies to any face, fingerprint, voiceprint, iris, or hand scan, including features like face-based photo tagging, voice login, or ID verification.
- Public written policy with a retention schedule and destruction rules
- Written notice of what is collected, why, and for how long, then a signed written release (electronic signature counts) before collecting
- Never sell, lease, trade, or profit from biometric data
- No disclosure to anyone, vendors included, without consent (narrow exceptions: completing a financial transaction the person requested, legal requirement, or a warrant or subpoena)
- Destroy biometric data when the purpose is met or within 3 years of the user's last interaction, whichever comes first
- Store and protect it at least as well as other confidential data
Private right of action: $1,000 per negligent violation or $5,000 per intentional or reckless violation (or actual damages if higher), plus attorneys' fees. Since August 2024, repeated scans of the same person by the same method count as one violation, so exposure is roughly per person, per violation type. Get this right before launch.

laws.name: Indiana Consumer Data Protection Act
laws.threshold: Controllers processing data of 100K+ IN consumers/year, or 25K+ IN consumers/year and deriving over 50% of revenue from personal data sales
laws.summary: Indiana's comprehensive privacy law, effective January 1, 2026. Closely modeled on Virginia's VCDPA. Opt-in consent for sensitive data; data protection assessments required. Correction right limited to data the consumer provided. AG enforces with a permanent 30-day cure period; up to $7,500 per violation.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice listing data categories, purposes, third parties, and how to exercise rights
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, and data copy, with identity verification and a 45-day response clock
- Appeal process for denied requests
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and significant-decision profiling
- Opt-in consent screen before collecting sensitive data
- Data protection assessment before launching targeted ads, data sales, profiling, or sensitive-data features
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you

laws.name: Iowa Consumer Data Protection Act
laws.threshold: Controllers processing data of 100K+ IA consumers/year, or 25K+ IA consumers/year and deriving over 50% of gross revenue from personal data sales
laws.summary: Iowa's privacy law, effective January 1, 2025. One of the more limited state laws — no correction right, no right to opt out of profiling, and no standalone right to opt out of targeted advertising (though businesses that do targeted advertising must clearly disclose it and how consumers can opt out), no data protection assessment requirement, and sensitive data requires opt-out (not opt-in). 90-day cure period (longest of any state law). AG enforces; civil penalties up to $7,500 per violation.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice listing data categories, purposes, third parties, and how to exercise rights
- Request flow for access, deletion, and portability with a 90-day response clock and appeal process
- Opt-out of sale, plus a clear and conspicuous disclosure if you sell data or run targeted ads, explaining how consumers can opt out
- Clear notice and an opt-out before processing sensitive data (Iowa does not require opt-in)
- Reasonable data security
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you

laws.name: Kentucky Consumer Data Protection Act
laws.threshold: Controllers processing data of 100K+ KY consumers/year, or 25K+ KY consumers/year and deriving over 50% of revenue from personal data sales
laws.summary: Kentucky's comprehensive privacy law, effective January 1, 2026. Closely modeled on Virginia's VCDPA. Consent required for sensitive data; data protection assessments required. AG enforces with a permanent 30-day cure period; up to $7,500 for each continued violation.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice listing data categories, purposes, third parties, and how to exercise rights
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, and portability, with identity verification and a 45-day response clock
- Appeal process for denied requests
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and significant-decision profiling
- Consent screen before collecting sensitive data
- Data protection assessment before launching targeted ads, data sales, risky profiling, or sensitive-data features (applies to processing activities created on or after June 1, 2026)
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you
laws.next: July 1, 2027: HB 692 bars collecting automatic content recognition (ACR) data from smart TVs and monitors without the consumer's consent.

laws.name: Maryland Online Data Privacy Act
laws.threshold: Businesses that controlled or processed data of at least 35,000 MD consumers in the prior calendar year (not counting data processed solely to complete a payment transaction), or at least 10,000 MD consumers and derived more than 20% of gross revenue from selling personal data
laws.summary: Maryland's comprehensive privacy law, effective October 1, 2025. One of the most protective state laws — prohibits processing of sensitive data unless strictly necessary (stronger than opt-in consent). Also bans selling sensitive data outright, even with consent. Requires data minimization: controllers may only process data that is reasonably necessary and proportionate. HB 711 (effective July 1, 2026) treats inferences that reveal a sensitive characteristic as sensitive data. It also bars selling personal data when the controller knew or should have known the buyer plans to use it for immigration enforcement, and bars knowingly selling personal data to a federal, state, or local government unit that engaged in or supported civil immigration enforcement within the 6 months before the sale. AG enforces; for violations on or before April 1, 2027, the AG's Consumer Protection Division may, at its discretion, issue a notice of violation giving at least 60 days to cure; civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation and up to $25,000 for each repeat of the same violation.
laws.build:
- Collect only data that is reasonably necessary and proportionate to the service the user asked for; this is a hard limit, not a disclosure
- Sensitive data: collect or process only when strictly necessary to provide the requested service; consent does not cure it
- Never sell sensitive data
- No sale or targeted advertising to users you know, or should have known, are under 18
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and profiling; honor universal opt-out signals
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, portability, and a list of the categories of third parties you disclosed data to, with a 45-day clock and an appeal process (60 days to decide appeals)
- Data protection assessment for each algorithm used in high-risk processing
- Applies to processing activities from April 1, 2026; audit existing data flows against the necessity standard
laws.next: April 1, 2027: the discretionary 60-day cure period ends for violations after that date (§ 14-4714).

laws.name: Minnesota Consumer Data Privacy Act
laws.threshold: Entities that control or process data of 100,000+ MN consumers in a calendar year (not counting data processed solely to complete a payment transaction), or that process data of 25,000+ MN consumers and derive over 25% of gross revenue from selling personal data. SBA small businesses are exempt but may not sell sensitive data without prior consent.
laws.summary: Minnesota's comprehensive privacy law, effective July 31, 2025. Adds a right to a list of specific third parties that received a consumer's data, a right to question profiling decisions, and a written data inventory requirement. Controllers must give a reason when denying a request. Opt-in for sensitive data and data protection assessments. AG enforces; the 30-day cure period ended January 31, 2026. Civil penalties up to $7,500 per violation.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice listing data categories, purposes, third parties, and how to exercise rights
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, and portability with a 45-day clock; explain the reason when denying a request and offer an appeal (45 days to decide, extendable by 60), keeping appeal records for 24 months
- List of specific third parties that received a consumer's data, available on request
- Right to question profiling results: tell users the reason for a significant decision and let them review data and request re-evaluation
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and profiling; honor universal opt-out signals
- Opt-in consent for sensitive data (parental consent under COPPA for known children under 13); no sale or targeted ads without consent for users you know are between the ages of 13 and 16
- Written data inventory and documented privacy and security policies
- Data protection assessment before high-risk processing
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you
laws.next: July 31, 2029: postsecondary institutions regulated by the Office of Higher Education must comply.

checker.dutyBelow: SBA small businesses that fall outside the law must still get prior consent before selling sensitive data (Minn. Stat. § 325M.17).

laws.name: Montana Consumer Data Privacy Act
laws.threshold: As amended by SB 297 (effective Oct 1, 2025): businesses that control or process data of at least 25,000 MT consumers (not counting data processed solely to complete a payment transaction), or at least 15,000 MT consumers and derive more than 25% of gross revenue from selling personal data. The minors' protections apply to any business operating in Montana or intentionally targeting Montana residents, regardless of size.
laws.summary: Montana's comprehensive privacy law, effective October 1, 2024, and significantly amended by SB 297 effective October 1, 2025. The amendment cut the threshold from 50K to 25K consumers, eliminated the cure period entirely, limited the entity-level financial exemption to banks, credit unions, and their financial affiliates (other GLBA data stays exempt at the data level), narrowed the nonprofit exemption, added a duty of care and consent rules for minors under 18, required a labeled opt-out link, and barred disclosing SSNs and account numbers in access responses. Requires opt-in consent for sensitive data. AG enforces with no cure period; SB 297 added civil penalties of up to $7,500 per violation.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice with the content required by the 2025 amendment, including a clearly labeled opt-out link
- Notify users of material privacy changes and let them withdraw earlier consent
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, and portability with a 45-day clock and appeal process
- Never return SSNs, account numbers, or similar identifiers in access responses
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and profiling; honor universal opt-out signals
- Opt-in consent for sensitive data
- If you know or willfully disregard that a user is under 18: use reasonable care to avoid heightened risk of harm, and get consent (a parent's for under 13) before targeted ads, sale, or significant-decision profiling, collecting precise geolocation not reasonably necessary, keeping data longer than needed, or using design features that extend use. These rules apply regardless of the size thresholds
- Data protection assessment for any online service, product, or feature that poses a heightened risk of harm to minors
- Data protection assessment before high-risk processing
- No cure period: the AG can act on the first violation

laws.name: Nebraska Data Privacy Act
laws.threshold: Any business processing Nebraska residents' data that is not an SBA-defined small business. No consumer-count or revenue threshold. Small businesses still need consent to sell sensitive data.
laws.summary: Nebraska's comprehensive privacy law, effective January 1, 2025. Follows the Texas model: coverage depends on not being an SBA small business rather than on user counts. Opt-in consent for sensitive data, data protection assessments for high-risk processing. AG enforces with a permanent 30-day cure period; up to $7,500 per violation.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice listing data categories, purposes, third parties, and how to exercise rights
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, and data copy, with identity verification and a 45-day response clock
- Appeal process for denied requests
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and significant-decision profiling; honor browser or device opt-out signals (like GPC) sent as an authorized agent, at least wherever you already honor them for other states
- Opt-in consent screen before collecting sensitive data (health, precise location, biometrics, race, religion, sexual orientation, immigration status, children's data)
- Data protection assessment before launching targeted ads, data sales, profiling, or sensitive-data features
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you

checker.dutyBelow: SBA small businesses must still get the consumer's prior consent before selling sensitive data (Neb. Rev. Stat. § 87-1118).

laws.name: New Hampshire Privacy Act
laws.threshold: Controllers processing data of 35K+ NH consumers/year (excluding data processed solely to complete a payment transaction), or 10K+ NH consumers/year and deriving more than 25% of gross revenue from personal data sales
laws.summary: New Hampshire's comprehensive privacy law, effective January 1, 2025. Closely modeled on Connecticut's CTDPA. Requires opt-in for sensitive data, data protection assessments for high-risk processing, and honoring universal opt-out signals. AG enforces with a mandatory 60-day cure period that ran through December 31, 2025; since January 1, 2026, a cure opportunity is at the AG's discretion. Civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice listing data categories, purposes, third parties, and how to exercise rights
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, and portability with a 45-day clock and appeal process
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and profiling; honor universal opt-out signals
- Opt-in consent for sensitive data
- Consent before selling or targeting ads to consumers you know are 13-15
- Data protection assessment before high-risk processing
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you
laws.next: January 1, 2027: HB 1460 bans selling personal data of children under 13, even with parental consent.

laws.name: New Jersey Data Privacy Act
laws.enforcer: New Jersey Division of Consumer Affairs (Attorney General)
laws.threshold: Controllers processing data of 100K+ NJ consumers/year (excluding data processed solely to complete a payment transaction), or 25K+ NJ consumers/year and deriving any revenue, or receiving a discount on goods or services, from personal data sales
laws.summary: New Jersey's comprehensive privacy law, effective January 15, 2025. Any revenue from selling personal data triggers coverage at 25K consumers, with no percentage floor. Broad sensitive data definition that includes financial information. Opt-in for sensitive data; assessments before high-risk processing starts. A5328 (P.L.2026, c.25, signed and effective June 30, 2026) bans selling sensitive data outright, with no consent exception, regardless of how many consumers' data a business handles (the NJDPA's existing exemptions still apply). Selling, offering for sale or licensing sensitive data carries a civil penalty of $50,000 per record. It also creates a data broker registry, with registration open April 1 to June 30, 2027. AG enforces under the Consumer Fraud Act (up to $10,000 for a first violation and $20,000 for each subsequent one); no private right of action. The 30-day cure period ended in July 2026.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice listing data categories, purposes, third parties, and how to exercise rights
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, and portability with a 45-day clock and appeal process
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and profiling; honor universal opt-out signals (required since July 15, 2025)
- Opt-in consent for sensitive data, which includes financial information and status as transgender or non-binary
- Do not sell sensitive data (health, financial, precise geolocation, biometric, known children's data and the other listed categories) to anyone, even with the consumer's consent
- Consent before selling, targeting ads to, or profiling (for legal or similarly significant decisions) consumers you know, or willfully disregard, are 13-16
- Data protection assessment before starting high-risk processing, not after
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you
laws.next: March 27, 2027: A5328 data broker and data collector registry provisions become operative; Division says initial registration runs April 1 to June 30, 2027. The Division's proposed NJDPA regulations (June 2, 2025) expired unadopted on June 2, 2026; a new proposal may follow.

checker.dutyBelow: Selling sensitive data is banned regardless of how many New Jersey consumers' data you handle, even with consent, unless an NJDPA exemption applies (A5328, June 30, 2026; $50,000 per record).

laws.name: Oklahoma Consumer Data Privacy Act
laws.threshold: Businesses that do business in Oklahoma or target products or services to Oklahoma residents and, in a calendar year, control or process personal data of at least 100,000 Oklahoma consumers, or at least 25,000 Oklahoma consumers while deriving over 50% of gross revenue from the sale of personal data. "Sale" means an exchange for monetary consideration only. Consumers acting in a commercial or employment context don't count. Exempt: state agencies and political subdivisions, GLBA financial institutions, HIPAA covered entities and business associates, nonprofits, and higher education institutions
laws.summary: Oklahoma's comprehensive privacy law, signed March 20, 2026 and effective January 1, 2027. It follows the Virginia model closely and is one of the more business-friendly state laws: "sale" covers only exchanges for money, there's no requirement to honor universal opt-out signals like GPC, and there are no authorized-agent provisions. Grants access, correction, deletion, portability, and opt-outs for sale, targeted advertising, and significant profiling. Sensitive data needs opt-in consent, and data from a known child under 13 must be handled under COPPA. No special teen rules. The AG enforces exclusively with a 30-day cure period that doesn't sunset; civil penalties up to $7,500 per violation, plus attorney fees and investigation costs. No private right of action.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice listing data categories, purposes, how to exercise rights and appeal, and data categories and third parties you share with
- At least two secure, reliable ways to submit requests (an online-only business with a direct consumer relationship can offer just an email address)
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, and portability with a 45-day response clock (one 45-day extension if you tell the consumer within the first 45 days); free up to twice a year
- Appeal process with a written decision within 60 days; if you deny an appeal, give the consumer a way to contact the Oklahoma AG
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and profiling with legal or similarly significant effects
- Opt-in consent before processing sensitive data; for a known child under 13, follow COPPA
- Consent before using data for purposes not reasonably necessary to or compatible with the ones you disclosed
- Data protection assessment before targeted advertising, sale, risky profiling, sensitive data processing, or other high-risk processing
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you

laws.name: Oregon Consumer Privacy Act
laws.threshold: Controllers processing data of 100K+ OR consumers/year (excluding payment-only data), or 25K+ OR consumers/year and deriving 25%+ of gross revenue from personal data sales
laws.summary: Oregon's comprehensive privacy law, effective July 1, 2024. Covers nonprofits beginning July 1, 2025 (most state laws exempt them). Consumers can get a list of the specific third parties that received their data. HB 2008 (2025), effective January 1, 2026, bans selling precise geolocation data (within 1,750 feet) for any consumer, and bans selling, targeted advertising to, or significant-decision profiling of consumers you know or willfully disregard are under 16, with no consent exception. Requires opt-in for sensitive data and honoring universal opt-out signals. AG enforces; no private right of action. 30-day cure ended January 1, 2026.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice listing data categories, purposes, third parties, and how to exercise rights
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, and portability with a 45-day clock and appeal process
- List of the specific third parties that received a consumer's data, available on request
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and profiling; honor universal opt-out signals
- Opt-in consent for sensitive data
- Do not sell precise geolocation data (within 1,750 feet) about anyone, and do not sell, target ads to, or profile (for legal or similarly significant decisions) consumers you know or willfully disregard are under 16; consent doesn't cure this (HB 2008, effective January 1, 2026)
- Data protection assessment before high-risk processing
- Nonprofits are covered: don't assume an exemption
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you

checker.dutyBelow: Motor vehicle manufacturers and their affiliates are covered at any volume if they process personal data from a consumer's use of a vehicle or vehicle component (HB 3875, effective September 26, 2025).

laws.name: Rhode Island Data Transparency and Privacy Protection Act
laws.threshold: Controllers processing data of 35K+ RI consumers/year (excluding payment-only data), or 10K+ RI consumers/year and deriving over 20% of revenue from personal data sales. Commercial websites and ISPs that collect, store and sell RI customers' personal data must post a notice regardless of size.
laws.summary: Rhode Island's comprehensive privacy law, effective January 1, 2026. Low thresholds (35K consumers). Opt-in for sensitive data; data protection assessments; privacy notice must name third parties data is sold to. A separate notice duty applies to any commercial website or ISP that sells Rhode Island customers' personal data, regardless of size. AG enforces with no cure period. Violations are deceptive trade practices (up to $10,000 per violation under R.I. Gen. Laws 6-13.1-8), plus a fine of $100 to $500 for each intentional disclosure of personal data in violation of the act.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice listing data categories collected and every third party you sell to or may sell to (required for any commercial website or ISP that sells RI customers' data, even below the thresholds)
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, and portability, with identity verification and a 45-day response clock
- Appeal process for denied requests
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and significant-decision profiling
- Opt-in consent screen before collecting sensitive data
- Data protection assessment before high-risk processing
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you
- No cure period: ship compliant, there is no warning letter

checker.dutyBelow: Any commercial website or internet service provider that collects, stores and sells Rhode Island customers' personal data must post a notice listing the data categories it collects, every third party it has sold or may sell to, and a contact email or online mechanism, even below the thresholds.

laws.name: Tennessee Information Protection Act
laws.threshold: Businesses in Tennessee (or targeting Tennessee residents) with more than $25M in revenue that either control or process data of at least 175,000 TN consumers in a calendar year, or control or process data of at least 25,000 TN consumers and derive more than 50% of gross revenue from selling personal information
laws.summary: Tennessee's comprehensive privacy law, effective July 1, 2025. Unique feature: an affirmative defense for companies that keep and follow a written privacy program that reasonably conforms to the NIST Privacy Framework (or comparable documented standards). The more-than-$25M revenue floor limits applicability to larger companies. 60-day cure period with no sunset. The AG has exclusive enforcement authority; civil penalties up to $7,500 per violation, and a court may award treble damages for willful or knowing violations. No private right of action.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice listing data categories, purposes, third parties, and how to exercise rights
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, and portability with a 45-day clock and appeal process
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and profiling
- Opt-in consent for sensitive data
- Data protection assessment before high-risk processing
- Reasonable administrative, technical, and physical data security
- Optional but valuable: a written privacy program that reasonably conforms to the NIST Privacy Framework (and is updated within two years of any new version) gives you an affirmative defense
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you

laws.name: Texas Data Privacy and Security Act
laws.threshold: Any entity that conducts business in Texas or produces products/services consumed by TX residents and processes personal data — no revenue or volume thresholds (broad applicability); small businesses as defined by SBA are exempt
laws.summary: Texas's comprehensive state privacy law, effective July 1, 2024. Notable for having no revenue or data volume thresholds — any business processing TX resident data that isn't a small business may be covered. Grants access, correction, deletion, portability, and opt-out rights (sale, targeted advertising, profiling). AG enforces with 30-day cure period; civil penalties up to $7,500 per violation. Universal opt-out mechanism must be honored.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice listing data categories, purposes, third parties, and how to exercise rights
- If you sell sensitive data, the exact notice text: "NOTICE: We may sell your sensitive personal data." (Biometric sales need their own version)
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, and portability with a 45-day response clock and appeal process
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and profiling; honor universal opt-out signals
- Opt-in consent before processing sensitive data; even SBA small businesses must get consent before selling sensitive data
- Data protection assessment before high-risk processing
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you

laws.name: Utah Consumer Privacy Act
laws.enforcer: Utah Attorney General / Division of Consumer Protection
laws.threshold: Controllers with $25M+ annual revenue that either control or process data of 100,000+ UT consumers in a calendar year, or derive over 50% of gross revenue from selling personal data and control or process data of 25,000+ UT consumers
laws.summary: Utah's privacy law, effective December 31, 2023. The most business-friendly state law: requires $25M revenue plus a volume threshold, has no data protection assessment requirement, and sensitive data needs only notice and an opt-out. A right to correct took effect July 1, 2026 (HB 418, 2025). Permanent 30-day cure period. The Division of Consumer Protection investigates and refers cases; the AG has exclusive enforcement authority and can recover actual damages plus civil penalties up to $7,500 per violation.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice listing data categories, purposes, third parties, and how to exercise rights
- Request flow for access, correction (since July 1, 2026), deletion of data the consumer provided, and portability, with a 45-day response clock (one 45-day extension allowed)
- Opt-out controls for sale and targeted advertising
- Clear notice and an opt-out before processing sensitive data (Utah does not require opt-in)
- Reasonable data security
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you
laws.next: January 1, 2027: HB 357 applies the UCPA to motor vehicle manufacturers that sell or lease vehicles in Utah and collect vehicle data, regardless of the usual thresholds; model year 2030 and later vehicles need in-vehicle privacy controls. July 1, 2027: the Digital Choice Act (social media data portability) takes effect after HB 408 delayed it a year.

laws.name: Virginia Consumer Data Protection Act
laws.threshold: Businesses in Virginia (or targeting Virginia residents) that control or process data of 100K+ VA consumers in a calendar year, or 25K+ VA consumers and derive over 50% of gross revenue from selling personal data
laws.summary: Virginia's comprehensive state privacy law, effective January 1, 2023. Grants consumers rights to access, correct, delete, port, and opt out of sale, targeted advertising, and profiling. Controllers must conduct data protection assessments for high-risk processing. No private right of action; the AG enforces with a 30-day cure period and up to $7,500 per violation. Entity-level exemptions for government bodies, GLBA financial institutions, HIPAA covered entities and business associates, nonprofits, and institutions of higher education. Since January 1, 2025, known children (under 13) get extra protections: no targeted ads, sale, or significant-decision profiling; precise geolocation only when reasonably necessary, with a visible signal; and COPPA parental consent for both. SB 338 (effective July 1, 2026) bans selling precise geolocation data (within 1,750 feet) of any consumer. SB 854's one-hour daily social media limit for users under 16 (effective January 1, 2026) is blocked by a preliminary injunction issued February 27, 2026; the Fourth Circuit denied a stay and calendared Virginia's appeal (NetChoice v. Jones, No. 26-1252) for oral argument on October 28, 2026.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice listing data categories, purposes, third parties, and how to exercise rights
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, and portability, with identity verification and a 45-day response clock
- Appeal process for denied requests, with a link to the AG complaint form
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and significant-decision profiling
- Opt-in consent screen before processing sensitive data; COPPA-compliant parental consent for known children under 13
- For known children: no targeted ads, sale, or significant-decision profiling; collect precise geolocation only when reasonably necessary, only as long as needed, with a signal shown to the child the whole time
- Never sell precise geolocation data (within 1,750 feet) of any consumer (since July 1, 2026)
- Data protection assessment before launching targeted ads, data sales, profiling, or sensitive-data features
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you

laws.name: Washington My Health My Data Act
laws.enforcer: Washington Attorney General (Consumer Protection Act); private lawsuits by injured consumers
laws.threshold: Any legal entity that does business in Washington or targets products or services to Washington consumers and, alone or with others, decides why and how consumer health data is collected, processed, shared or sold. No revenue or volume threshold. "Consumer" means a Washington resident or anyone whose health data is collected in Washington, acting in a personal or household context (not employees). Small businesses (fewer than 100,000 consumers' health data in a calendar year, or less than 50% of gross revenue from consumer health data and fewer than 25,000 consumers) are covered too; they just had until June 30, 2024. The geofencing ban applies to any person. Excludes government agencies, tribal nations and their contracted service providers, and data already covered by HIPAA, GLBA, FCRA, FERPA and similar regimes.
laws.summary: Washington's consumer health data law, not a comprehensive privacy law. Obligations started March 31, 2024 (June 30, 2024 for small businesses). The geofencing ban took effect July 23, 2023. "Consumer health data" is broad: conditions, medications, symptoms, reproductive and gender-affirming care, biometric and genetic data, precise location that could show someone seeking care, and health inferences drawn from non-health data (for example by algorithms). There's no size threshold. You need separate opt-in consent to collect and to share health data, unless it's necessary for a service the consumer asked for, and a signed written authorization from the consumer to sell it. You need a standalone Consumer Health Data Privacy Policy linked from your homepage. Geofences within 2,000 feet of an in-person health care provider can't be used to track visitors, collect their health data or target them with health messages or ads. Violations count as violations of the Consumer Protection Act, so the AG can sue (up to $7,500 per violation) and injured consumers can sue for actual damages, attorney fees and up to triple damages capped at $25,000. No cure period.
laws.build:
- Standalone Consumer Health Data Privacy Policy with its own prominent homepage link, listing categories collected, purposes and uses, sources, categories shared, the third parties and specific affiliates you share with, and how to exercise rights
- Separate opt-in consent to collect consumer health data, unless collection is necessary to provide a product or service the consumer asked for
- A second, separate opt-in consent to share consumer health data, distinct from the collection consent
- Consent requests that state the categories, purpose and uses, types of recipients, and how to withdraw; no consent through broad terms of use, hovering or closing content, or dark patterns
- New disclosure and fresh consent before collecting new categories of health data or using it for new purposes
- Signed, standalone written authorization before selling consumer health data, naming the buyer and seller and expiring after one year; keep copies for six years
- Request flow to confirm and access health data, including a list of all third parties and affiliates you shared or sold it with and their contact details
- Withdrawal of consent to collection and sharing
- Deletion that reaches archives and backups (within six months) and notice to all affiliates, processors, contractors and third parties so they delete too
- 45-day response clock, one 45-day extension with notice, and no new account required to submit a request
- Appeal process with a written answer within 45 days and AG contact info if you deny it
- No geofencing within 2,000 feet of in-person health care providers to track visitors, collect their health data, or send health-related messages or ads
- Access limited to staff and processors who need it, plus reasonable data security
- Binding contracts with every processor that handles health data for you
- No discrimination against consumers for exercising their rights
